  "title": "Representation-Grounded Diversity Selection with Collapse-Aware Failsafe for Iterative Synthetic Training",
  "core_problem": "Current synthetic data filtering for iterative training treats diversity measurement as static: methods either use quality-only criteria (self-verification, perplexity thresholds) or measure diversity in fixed external embedding spaces (cluster membership, sentence embeddings). Neither captures how the student model's own representation space evolves and progressively collapses across training generations — yet this representational collapse is precisely the mechanism driving model collapse, as proven by the Strong Model Collapse result (ICLR 2025). Moreover, methods that do use model-internal representations (DiverseEvol, SAE-based diversity) operate in single-iteration settings and assume the representation space remains trustworthy — but in iterative training, representations themselves degrade, creating a fundamental paradox: the very space used to measure diversity becomes less reliable as collapse progresses. No existing method addresses this paradox by jointly tracking representation quality and diversity across generations.",
  "opportunity": "The Strong Model Collapse paper proves collapse stems from tail distribution erosion across generations. Several recent works address quality-diversity tradeoffs in data selection: DCES (Electronics 2025) uses cluster-based center-edge sampling with dynamic ratios; Quad (ICLR 2025 Spotlight) combines influence-based quality with cluster diversity via multi-armed bandits; DiSF (ICLR 2026 Oral) achieves eigenvalue uniformity in feature covariance via greedy submodular selection using Contriever embeddings; DiverseEvol uses model-internal embeddings for instruction tuning; SAE-based diversity (arXiv:2502.14050) uses sparse autoencoder features from a separate model for diversity-driven data selection. However, all these methods either (a) operate in fixed external embedding spaces that cannot track the student model's evolving collapse trajectory (DCES, Quad, DiSF, SAE-based diversity), (b) target pretraining or single-iteration selection rather than multi-generation iterative training (Quad, DiSF, DiverseEvol, SAE-based diversity), or (c) lack quality-diversity integration in the collapse context (DiverseEvol). The critical missing piece is a representation quality monitor: recent work on capability emergence (arXiv:2602.15997) shows that representation collapse is gradual, measurable via effective rank (RankMe), and precedes behavioral degradation — meaning there exists a window where model-internal representations are collapsing but still discriminative enough to be useful for diversity scoring. This creates a concrete opportunity: use model-internal diversity scoring during the window when it is most informative (early-to-mid collapse), and fall back to external embeddings when representation quality degrades past a critical threshold. Additionally, 'What Matters in LLM-generated Data' (arXiv:2506.19262) demonstrates that the diversity-performance relationship is non-monotonic in single-round settings — combining model-internal diversity measurement with collapse-adaptive scheduling and a quality-aware failsafe would create the first method that tracks and counteracts collapse from the student model's own perspective while accounting for both the benefits and risks of using degenerating representations.",
  "landscape": "Self-verification (NeurIPS 2025) filters by model confidence and provably prevents collapse under accurate confidence assumptions, but ignores diversity entirely. DCES ('Countering Model Collapse via Dynamic Center-Edge Sampling', Electronics 2025) uses cluster-based sampling that preserves edge/tail samples with quality filtering and dynamic ratio adjustment — the closest prior work on iterative collapse, but relies on external clustering (k-means in sentence embedding space) with coarse center-edge boundaries rather than continuous, model-internal diversity scoring. Quad ('Harnessing Diversity for Important Data Selection', ICLR 2025 Spotlight) jointly optimizes quality (attention-layer influence) and diversity (cluster exploration via multi-armed bandits) but targets pretraining data selection, not iterative synthetic training collapse. DiSF ('Combatting Dimensional Collapse via Diversified File Selection', ICLR 2026 Oral) achieves eigenvalue uniformity in feature covariance via greedy submodular selection using Contriever embeddings — the most scalable diversity selection method and our primary methodological inspiration, but uses fixed Contriever embeddings and targets pretraining dimensional collapse, not iterative model collapse across generations. DiverseEvol (arXiv:2311.08182) uses the model's own embedding space for diversity-driven iterative data selection with Vendi Score, but operates in single-iteration instruction tuning without multi-generation collapse tracking or representation quality monitoring. SAE-based diversity (arXiv:2502.14050, 'Diversity-driven Data Selection via Sparse Autoencoder') uses sparse autoencoder features for diversity-aware data selection — a model-internal feature approach, but uses a separately trained SAE on a different model (Llama-3.1-8B), not the student model's own evolving representations, and targets single-iteration instruction tuning. SPICE ('Submodular Penalized Information-Conflict Selection', arXiv:2601.23155, ICLR 2026) maximizes log-determinant Fisher information with gradient conflict penalization — a principled submodular selection approach but targeting instruction tuning efficiency, not iterative collapse prevention. DCScore (arXiv:2502.08512, ICML 2025) proposes classification-based diversity measurement for synthetic datasets with O(n²) complexity and axiomatic foundations — relevant as an evaluation metric but not designed for generation-aware selection. 'Less is Enough' (arXiv:2602.10388, Feb 2026) proposes Feature Activation Coverage using sparse autoencoder features for model-internal diversity measurement, but for one-shot data synthesis, not iterative collapse prevention. 'Rethinking Representativeness and Diversity in Dynamic Data Selection' (arXiv:2603.04981, Mar 2026) redefines diversity as process-level trajectory over training with a frequency-penalty mechanism using SAE features — conceptually related but targets within-epoch data selection, not cross-generation iterative collapse. DCE ('Dynamic Context Evolution', arXiv:2604.07147, Apr 2026) uses semantic memory and verbalized tail sampling for generation-time diversity but addresses cross-batch mode collapse during inference, not training-time iterative collapse. 'Representation Collapse in Machine Translation Through the Lens of Angular Dispersion' (EACL 2026 Findings, arXiv:2602.17287) demonstrates that representation collapse is gradual across training and measurable via angular dispersion — supporting our premise that collapse can be tracked before representations become uninformative. 'Anatomy of Capability Emergence' (arXiv:2602.15997, Feb 2026) shows that representations collapse to low-dimensional states (measurable via RankMe/effective rank) before recovering, and that geometric changes precede behavioral ones — directly supporting the existence of a window where collapsing representations remain discriminative. Quality-Weighted Vendi Score (ICML 2024) provides a principled joint quality-diversity metric but has not been applied to iterative synthetic training selection. 'What Matters in LLM-generated Data' (arXiv:2506.19262) finds moderately diverse data enhances performance but highly diverse data hurts — challenging monotonic diversity scheduling. ToEdit (ICML 2025) uses token-level editing to restore distributional properties but modifies data rather than selecting it. 'Synthetic Eggs in Many Baskets' (ACL 2026 Findings) shows multi-source generator diversity mitigates collapse but operates at the source level. 'A Closer Look at Model Collapse' (arXiv:2509.16499) proposes entropy-based greedy selection for diffusion model collapse and demonstrates the generalization-to-memorization transition is gradual. GEM ('Preserving Diversity in Supervised Fine-Tuning', ICLR 2025) addresses diversity preservation via training loss modification, a complementary approach to data selection. 'From Collapse to Improvement' (arXiv:2602.10531, Feb 2026) provides statistical perspectives on iterative training dynamics, showing improvement is possible with fresh real data. The LLM Data Auditor survey (arXiv:2601.17717) catalogs quality metrics and notes the gap in model-aware diversity evaluation. No existing work (a) grounds diversity measurement in the student model's own evolving representations while simultaneously monitoring representation quality to determine when those representations become unreliable, (b) provides a principled failsafe from model-internal to external embeddings based on representation quality degradation, or (c) combines these with collapse-adaptive scheduling in the multi-generation iterative training setting.",
  "approach": "We propose Representation-Grounded Diversity Selection (RGDS), a synthetic data selection pipeline that measures diversity in the student model's own evolving representation space to prevent collapse across iterative training generations, with a principled failsafe mechanism that detects when model-internal representations become too degraded and switches to external embeddings.

**Architecture Overview.** At each generation t, RGDS operates in five steps:

**(1) Representation extraction and quality assessment.** All candidate synthetic samples plus a fixed held-out reference set R (a random 5K-sample subset of the original human training data, held constant across all generations) are passed through the current student model M_{t-1}, extracting last-hidden-layer representations (dimension d_model ≈ 2048 for Qwen3-1.7B). We compute two representation quality metrics on R's representations: (a) effective rank via RankMe (Shannon entropy of normalized singular values of the representation matrix), and (b) k-NN probe accuracy — train a 5-NN classifier on R's representations to distinguish samples containing rare n-grams (bottom 10% frequency) from common ones, measuring whether the representation space still discriminates tail from center. These metrics quantify whether M_{t-1}'s representations remain trustworthy for diversity scoring.

**(2) Failsafe decision.** If effective rank drops below τ_rank = 50% of the generation-0 value, OR k-NN probe accuracy drops below τ_knn = 60% (near random for binary classification), RGDS switches to external embeddings (Contriever-110M, the same model used by DiSF) for the remaining steps. This resolves the representation degeneration paradox: RGDS uses model-internal diversity when it is most informative (early-to-mid collapse, when representations are degrading but still discriminative) and falls back to stable external representations when model-internal ones become unreliable. The failsafe thresholds are validated via ablation.

**(3) Dimensionality reduction.** PCA projection to d=32 dimensions, with PCA fitted on the reference set R's representations through the current embedding source (model-internal or Contriever, per step 2). Using a fixed reference set for PCA fitting ensures the projection basis is driven by the same data across generations, making eigenvalue uniformity measurements comparable. This eliminates the PCA basis drift problem: changes in eigenvalue uniformity across generations reflect model changes, not training data changes.

**(4) Diversity-quality joint selection.** A greedy submodular algorithm (adapted from DiSF) iteratively selects candidates that maximize covariance eigenvalue uniformity in the projected representation space, subject to a quality floor (perplexity under M_{t-1} must be below a generation-dependent threshold). The selection maximizes the proxy function F(S) = exp(-||C(S)||_F), where C(S) is the covariance matrix of selected samples' projected representations. Per DiSF's Lemma 1, minimizing ||C||_F² directly minimizes eigenvalue variance, promoting uniform eigenvalues. Quality floor: samples with perplexity above the 90th percentile of the reference set's perplexity under M_{t-1} are excluded. Complexity: O(|S|²·b·d²) per batch, independent of model embedding dimensionality.

**(5) Collapse-adaptive diversity scheduling.** Rather than a fixed diversity emphasis, RGDS monitors the eigenvalue uniformity ratio u_t of the reference set R's raw d_model-dimensional covariance matrix (no PCA, avoiding basis drift in the monitoring signal). The monitoring signal is EMA-smoothed with decay α=0.3 to prevent oscillation: ũ_t = α·u_t + (1-α)·ũ_{t-1}. The diversity weight λ_t (controlling the quality-diversity tradeoff in selection) follows: if ũ_t < 0.8·ũ_0 (uniformity dropped below 80% of initial), λ_t = min(λ_{t-1} · 1.5, λ_max); if ũ_t ≥ 0.9·ũ_0 (uniformity recovered to near-initial), λ_t = max(λ_{t-1} · 0.8, λ_min); otherwise, λ_t = λ_{t-1}. Default: λ_0 = 1.0, λ_min = 0.5, λ_max = 3.0. The EMA smoothing and multiplicative (rather than additive) adjustment with a dead zone between 0.8 and 0.9 prevents oscillation. This addresses the non-monotonic diversity finding from 'What Matters in LLM-generated Data' — diversity is intensified only when the model signals collapse, not as a default ramp.

**Resolving the Representation Degeneration Paradox.** The paper's core theoretical contribution addresses why model-internal diversity scoring works despite representation degradation:
(a) *Formal argument*: We prove that eigenvalue uniformity of the representation covariance is a valid diversity proxy as long as the representation function is injective on the support of the data distribution (i.e., distinct inputs map to distinct representations). Model collapse erodes the *tails* of the learned distribution (Strong Model Collapse, ICLR 2025), reducing effective rank, but the representation function remains injective — it loses tail *coverage* before losing *discriminability*. Eigenvalue uniformity decline is therefore an early warning of collapse, detectable before representations become uninformative.
(b) *Empirical validation*: A core experiment — the Representation Quality Monitor — plots at each generation: effective rank (RankMe), k-NN probe accuracy (rare vs. common n-gram discrimination), and rank correlation between model-internal and Contriever-based diversity scores. This directly characterizes the window of useful model-internal diversity scoring and validates the failsafe thresholds. Prior work supports this: 'Anatomy of Capability Emergence' (arXiv:2602.15997) shows representation geometry changes precede behavioral collapse, confirming a lag between representation degradation and functional failure.
(c) *Failsafe mechanism*: Even if the theoretical argument breaks down in practice, the failsafe (step 2) detects and handles the case, making RGDS robust regardless.

**Experimental Design.** We validate RGDS on iterative training loops using two model pairs:
- Primary: Qwen3-1.7B (student) / Qwen3-4B (fixed generator)
- Secondary: Pythia-1.4B (student) / Pythia-6.9B (fixed generator) — different model family to test generalizability

Three datasets:
- WikiText-103 (encyclopedic text, standard model collapse benchmark)
- OpenWebText (diverse web text, using a 100M-token subset)
- PubMed abstracts (domain-specific biomedical text, ~10M-token subset)

Core methods (8 total, run for 8 generations, best 2 extended to 12):
1. RGDS (full method)
2. RGDS-external-only (ablation: Contriever embeddings throughout, no model-internal — isolates model-grounded contribution)
3. RGDS-no-failsafe (ablation: model-internal throughout, no failsafe — tests degeneration paradox empirically)
4. Periodically-updated Contriever (re-extract Contriever embeddings on current training set each generation — isolates whether advantage comes from tracking evolving data composition vs. model-internal representations)
5. Generator-model representations (use Qwen3-4B/Pythia-6.9B representations for diversity scoring — stable, non-collapsing space)
6. DCES (cluster-based center-edge sampling — strongest existing iterative collapse baseline)
7. Self-verification (quality-only — ablates diversity entirely)
8. Uncurated (no filtering)

Additional ablations: PCA dimensions (16, 32, 64), fixed vs. adaptive diversity scheduling, failsafe threshold sensitivity (τ_rank ∈ {0.3, 0.5, 0.7}, τ_knn ∈ {0.55, 0.60, 0.65}), and EMA decay sensitivity (α ∈ {0.1, 0.3, 0.5}).

Collapse metrics:
- Rare n-gram survival rate (tail preservation)
- Quality-Weighted Vendi Score trajectory (ICML 2024)
- DCScore (ICML 2025) (classification-based diversity)
- Downstream perplexity on held-out data
- Representation Quality Monitor curves (RankMe effective rank + k-NN probe accuracy across generations)
- Covariance eigenvalue uniformity trajectory",

## Reviewer feedback (round 3)
Issues: ["CRITICAL — VENUE MISMATCH: The user's hard requirement is EMNLP 2026 (ARR deadline May 25, 2026, 16 days away), but the proposal explicitly states EMNLP 2026 is 'no longer feasible' and targets AAAI 2027. This directly violates the user's stated goal. The experimental scope expanded beyond EMNLP feasibility in response to Round 2 reviewer feedback (add more datasets, add second model pair) — but the user's constraints should take priority over scope expansion.", "CRITICAL — COMPUTE/TIMELINE VIOLATION: User constraint is ≤200 H100-hours in ≤16 days. Manual mode estimates ~200h over 7-9 weeks; HIL estimates ~250h over 4-6 weeks. Even manual mode exceeds the 16-day timeline by 4-7x. The 8 methods × 8-12 generations × 3 datasets × 2 model pairs experimental matrix requires ~150+ sequential GPU-days across chains, fundamentally incompatible with a 16-day window even with aggressive parallelism.", "MISSING RELATED WORK — DaaR (arXiv:2502.04380, 'Diversity as a Reward: Fine-Tuning LLMs on a Mixture of Domain-Undetermined Data', Feb 2025): Uses the LLM's own embedding-layer representations for self-supervised diversity estimation in iterative fine-tuning with a closed-loop framework. Achieves SOTA across 7 benchmarks. This is the closest existing work to RGDS's core claim of using model-internal representations for diversity-driven data selection and is NOT cited. The novelty positioning must address how RGDS differs from DaaR (key distinction: multi-generation collapse prevention + failsafe, vs. DaaR's single-phase fine-tuning).", "THEORETICAL WEAKNESS — The injectivity argument ('representation function remains injective — it loses tail coverage before losing discriminability') conflates mathematical injectivity with practical utility. An injective function can still map all points to a low-dimensional manifold where pairwise distances become uniformly small, making diversity scoring meaningless despite technical injectivity. The formal argument needs to bound the rate of distance distortion, not just assert injectivity. The empirical validation (Representation Quality Monitor) is the real safety net — the theoretical argument as stated would not survive a knowledgeable reviewer.", "HYPERPARAMETER PROLIFERATION — The method introduces at minimum 8 tunable hyperparameters: τ_rank, τ_knn, λ_0, λ_min, λ_max, α (EMA decay), PCA dimension d, and quality floor percentile. Even with the proposed ablation grid, the interaction space is large. This creates a risk that the method appears to 'work' primarily because of extensive hyperparameter tuning on the specific experimental setup, undermining generalizability claims.", "MINOR — Venue attribution errors: (1) DiSF is listed as 'ICLR 2026 Oral' but search results indicate it may be ICLR 2025 Oral (arXiv:2504.20644 submitted April 2025, conference proceedings suggest 2025). (2) Quad is listed as 'ICLR 2025 Spotlight' but OpenReview/proceedings list it as a poster. (3) DCES is listed as 'Electronics 2025' but MDPI metadata shows volume 15 issue 4 (2026). These don't affect the technical argument but damage credibility."]
Feedback: The core idea — grounding diversity measurement in the student model's own evolving representations with a quality-aware failsafe — is genuinely compelling and addresses a real gap. The Round 2 improvements (PCA basis drift fix, adaptive scheduling, failsafe thresholds) are well-executed. But the idea has drifted fatally from the user's requirements. Specific actions needed:

1. **RESTORE EMNLP 2026 TARGETING**: Scale the experimental scope back to fit ≤200 H100-hours in ≤16 days. Concrete proposal: (a) ONE model pair only (Qwen3-1.7B/4B — better supported, more relevant); (b) TWO datasets (WikiText-103 + one domain-specific); (c) FIVE methods (RGDS, RGDS-external-only, DCES, self-verification, uncurated); (d) 5-6 generations (sufficient to show collapse dynamics); (e) drop the second model pair entirely (mention as future work). This reduces compute to ~80-120 H100-hours, with ~80h for ablations, fitting the 200h budget. Sequential bottleneck: 5 methods × 2 datasets = 10 chains of ~5 generations × ~1.5h = ~75h wall-clock on a single GPU, or ~10h on 8 parallel GPUs, leaving 6+ days for analysis and paper writing.

2. **CITE AND DIFFERENTIATE FROM DaaR**: DaaR (arXiv:2502.04380) is the closest competitor — it uses the model's own embedding space for diversity-driven iterative data selection. Your key differentiators are: (a) multi-generation collapse prevention (DaaR targets single-phase fine-tuning), (b) representation quality monitoring + failsafe (DaaR assumes stable representations), (c) collapse-adaptive scheduling. State these explicitly.

3. **DROP THE FORMAL INJECTIVITY ARGUMENT**: The theoretical claim about injectivity is not rigorous enough for a top venue and will draw fire from reviewers. Instead, position the Representation Quality Monitor as the primary contribution: an empirical analysis tool that characterizes exactly when model-internal diversity scoring remains valid. The k-NN probe accuracy + RankMe curves across generations ARE the contribution — they replace the theoretical argument with direct evidence.

4. **REDUCE HYPERPARAMETERS**: Fix α=0.3 and d=32 as defaults (don't ablate). Fix quality floor at 90th percentile. This leaves τ_rank, τ_knn, λ_0 as the only tuned parameters, with λ_min and λ_max as sensitivity checks. Report sensitivity analysis in appendix, not main paper.

5. **VERIFY VENUE ATTRIBUTIONS**: Check and correct DiSF (2025 vs. 2026), Quad (Spotlight vs. Poster), and DCES (2025 vs. 2026) venue claims before submission.

## Instructions
- Think in two phases: FIRST reconsider the problem framing (core_problem / opportunity / landscape) if the reviewer flagged issues there, THEN revise the method (approach / resource_estimate / key_references). Do not jump straight to fixing the method if the underlying problem framing needs correction.
- Address each issue specifically.

## 深度调研要求（每一轮修订都必须执行）

不要简单地'打补丁'——每一轮修订都是重新审视和深化这个 idea 的机会。

1. **深度搜索**：针对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，建议用 2-3 种不同的搜索查询调研。
   - 搜索最新的相关论文（arXiv, conference proceedings）
   - 搜索 benchmark/leaderboard 确认当前 SOTA
   - 搜索可能遗漏的相关工作和 concurrent work

2. **深度阅读**：用 WebFetch 实际阅读找到的关键论文的 abstract 和方法部分，
   不要只依赖搜索摘要。形成你自己对领域现状的独立判断。

3. **深度思考**：在修订之前，先独立思考以下问题：
   - 这个 idea 的核心假设是否仍然成立？
   - reviewer 的批评是否揭示了更深层的问题？
   - 有没有更好的 framing 或 approach 来解决同一个核心问题？
   - 修订后的 idea 相比上一版有什么本质性的改进？

4. **避免表面修订**：如果你发现自己只是在换措辞或补充细节而没有实质改进，
   考虑是否需要 major revision 或 pivot。反复的 minor fix 不会拯救一个根基有问题的 idea。

  "approach": "We propose Representation-Grounded Diversity Selection (RGDS), a synthetic data selection pipeline that measures diversity in the student model's own evolving representation space to prevent collapse across iterative training generations, with a principled failsafe mechanism that detects when model-internal representations become too degraded and switches to external embeddings.

**Architecture Overview.** At each generation t, RGDS operates in five steps:

**(1) Representation extraction and quality assessment.** All candidate synthetic samples plus a fixed held-out reference set R (a random 5K-sample subset of the original human training data, held constant across all generations) are passed through the current student model M_{t-1}, extracting last-hidden-layer representations (dimension d_model ≈ 2048 for Qwen3-1.7B). **(2) Failsafe decision.** If effective rank drops below τ_rank = 50% of the generation-0 value, OR k-NN probe accuracy drops below τ_knn = 60% (near random for binary classification), RGDS switches to external embeddings (Contriever-110M, the same model used by DiSF) for the remaining steps. **(3) Dimensionality reduction.** PCA projection to d=32 dimensions, with PCA fitted on the reference set R's representations through the current embedding source (model-internal or Contriever, per step 2). Using a fixed reference set for PCA fitting ensures the projection basis is driven by the same data across generations, making eigenvalue uniformity measurements comparable. This eliminates the PCA basis drift problem: changes in eigenvalue uniformity across generations reflect model changes, not training data changes.

The selection maximizes the proxy function F(S) = exp(-||C(S)||_F), where C(S) is the covariance matrix of selected samples' projected representations. Per DiSF's Lemma 1, minimizing ||C||_F² directly minimizes eigenvalue variance, promoting uniform eigenvalues. Quality floor: samples with perplexity above the 90th percentile of the reference set's perplexity under M_{t-1} are excluded. Complexity: O(|S|²·b·d²) per batch, independent of model embedding dimensionality.

**(5) Collapse-adaptive diversity scheduling.** Rather than a fixed diversity emphasis, RGDS monitors the eigenvalue uniformity ratio u_t of the reference set R's raw d_model-dimensional covariance matrix (no PCA, avoiding basis drift in the monitoring signal). The monitoring signal is EMA-smoothed with decay α=0.3 to prevent oscillation: ũ_t = α·u_t + (1-α)·ũ_{t-1}. The diversity weight λ_t (controlling the quality-diversity tradeoff in selection) follows: if ũ_t < 0.8·ũ_0 (uniformity dropped below 80% of initial), λ_t = min(λ_{t-1} · 1.5, λ_max); if ũ_t ≥ 0.9·ũ_0 (uniformity recovered to near-initial), λ_t = max(λ_{t-1} · 0.8, λ_min); otherwise, λ_t = λ_{t-1}. Default: λ_0 = 1.0, λ_min = 0.5, λ_max = 3.0. The EMA smoothing and multiplicative (rather than additive) adjustment with a dead zone between 0.8 and 0.9 prevents oscillation. This addresses the non-monotonic diversity finding from 'What Matters in LLM-generated Data' — diversity is intensified only when the model signals collapse, not as a default ramp.

**Resolving the Representation Degeneration Paradox.** The paper's core theoretical contribution addresses why model-internal diversity scoring works despite representation degradation:
(a) *Formal argument*: We prove that eigenvalue uniformity of the representation covariance is a valid diversity proxy as long as the representation function is injective on the support of the data distribution (i.e., distinct inputs map to distinct representations). Model collapse erodes the *tails* of the learned distribution (Strong Model Collapse, ICLR 2025), reducing effective rank, but the representation function remains injective — it loses tail *coverage* before losing *discriminability*. Eigenvalue uniformity decline is therefore an early warning of collapse, detectable before representations become uninformative.
(b) *Empirical validation*: A core experiment — the Representation Quality Monitor — plots at each generation: effective rank (RankMe), k-NN probe accuracy (rare vs. common n-gram discrimination), and rank correlation between model-internal and Contriever-based diversity scores. This directly characterizes the window of useful model-internal diversity scoring and validates the failsafe thresholds. Prior work supports this: 'Anatomy of Capability Emergence' (arXiv:2602.15997) shows representation geometry changes precede behavioral collapse, confirming a lag between representation degradation and functional failure.
(c) *Failsafe mechanism*: Even if the theoretical argument breaks down in practice, the failsafe (step 2) detects and handles the case, making RGDS robust regardless.

**Experimental Design.** We validate RGDS on iterative training loops using two model pairs:
- Primary: Qwen3-1.7B (student) / Qwen3-4B (fixed generator)
- Secondary: Pythia-1.4B (student) / Pythia-6.9B (fixed generator) — different model family to test generalizability

Three datasets:
- WikiText-103 (encyclopedic text, standard model collapse benchmark)
- OpenWebText (diverse web text, using a 100M-token subset)
- PubMed abstracts (domain-specific biomedical text, ~10M-token subset)

Core methods (8 total, run for 8 generations, best 2 extended to 12):
1. RGDS (full method)
2. RGDS-external-only (ablation: Contriever embeddings throughout, no model-internal — isolates model-grounded contribution)
3. RGDS-no-failsafe (ablation: model-internal throughout, no failsafe — tests degeneration paradox empirically)
4. Periodically-updated Contriever (re-extract Contriever embeddings on current training set each generation — isolates whether advantage comes from tracking evolving data composition vs. model-internal representations)
5. Generator-model representations (use Qwen3-4B/Pythia-6.9B representations for diversity scoring — stable, non-collapsing space)
6. DCES (cluster-based center-edge sampling — strongest existing iterative collapse baseline)
7. Self-verification (quality-only — ablates diversity entirely)
8. Uncurated (no filtering)

- Rare n-gram survival rate (tail preservation)
- Quality-Weighted Vendi Score trajectory (ICML 2024)
- DCScore (ICML 2025) (classification-based diversity)
- Downstream perplexity on held-out data
- Representation Quality Monitor curves (RankMe effective rank + k-NN probe accuracy across generations)
- Covariance eigenvalue uniformity trajectory",

input.prompt: Extract the key technical details: 1) Exactly what embedding space does DaaR use for diversity measurement - the model's own hidden states? Which layer? 2) Is the method iterative (multiple rounds of selection and fine-tuning) or single-phase? 3) How does it measure diversity - what specific metric? 4) Does it monitor representation quality or have any failsafe mechanism? 5) What models and datasets were used in experiments? 6) What are the main limitations mentioned?

content.content:
# DaaR Technical Details Summary

## 1. Embedding Space for Diversity Measurement

DaaR uses **the LLM's own frozen hidden layer embeddings**. Specifically, the method operates on "the output of the embedding layer of the given LLM" and uses embeddings from a selected middle layer of the model. Appendix G.2 notes that "discrimination accuracy derived from layer 1-10 fluctuates in 91.2-93.6%," indicating flexibility in layer selection with minimal performance variation.

## 2. Iterative vs. Single-Phase Design

The approach is **single-phase with preparation stages**. It comprises: (1) model-aware centroid generation via two-phase synthesis (seed generation + diversity augmentation), (2) two-stage probe training (domain predictor, then diversity rewarding), and (3) final data selection. No iterative refinement loops occur after the initial selection.

## 3. Diversity Measurement Metric

DaaR uses **predictive entropy as the core diversity proxy**. The method trains an MLP probe (ψ_div) to estimate Shannon entropy: "H(x̃) = -∑p_k(x̃)log p_k(x̃)" where p_k represents domain classification probabilities. The paper notes this works better than direct diversity metrics because "models require sample-level processing unable to leverage pairwise relationships."

## 4. Representation Quality Monitoring

The method includes **stability mechanisms** but limited failsafes. It verifies: inter-centroid similarities >0.98 across runs, validation accuracy of 92.7% for domain classification, and final performance standard deviation of only 0.08. However, no dynamic adjustment triggers are described if quality degrades.

## 5. Experimental Setup

**Models tested**: Llama3.1-8B, Qwen2-7B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-8B, Llama3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-14B

**Training data**: 40,000 instruction pairs from Dolly-15k, CoT-en, Math-Instruct, Code-Alpaca (10,000 each)

**Benchmarks**: NQ, TriviaQA, Hellaswag, GSM8K, MATH, MBPP, HumanEval, MMLU

## 6. Main Limitations

- **Customization complexity**: "The customization of the selection ratios to support broader application in real-world scenarios" requires manual tuning
- **Hyperparameter sensitivity**: Multiple thresholds (similarity τ, diversity threshold) need setting
- **Scalability questions**: Method generates synthetic domain data via LLM prompting, adding computational overhead

## DiSF: "Combatting Dimensional Collapse in LLM Pre-Training Data via Diversified File Selection"

DiSF (DiverSified File selection algorithm) selects the most decorrelated text files in the feature space to prevent collapse and enhance diversity.

**Acceptance Status:** The paper was accepted to ICLR as an oral presentation (as noted in the GitHub repository title).

**Core Contribution:** The paper revisits recent innovations in file selection for pre-training LLMs and identifies a diversity dilemma called dimensional collapse, where performance improves on specific tasks but degrades overall across diverse tasks. DiSF addresses this by selecting decorrelated text files in the embedding space.

**Methodology:** The approach uses a classical greedy algorithm to achieve more uniform eigenvalues in the feature covariance matrix of the selected texts.

**Key Results:** DiSF saves 98.5% of 590M training files in SlimPajama, outperforming full-data pre-training within a 50B training budget, and achieving about 1.5x training efficiency and 5x data efficiency.

**Availability:** Source code is available at https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/DiSF.git

## Model Collapse Mechanisms and Prevention

Recent research identifies a transition from generalization to memorization during model collapse in diffusion models, where models increasingly replicate training data instead of generating novel content during iterative training on synthetic samples. This transition is directly driven by the declining entropy of the synthetic training data produced in each training cycle.

An entropy-based data selection strategy has been proposed to mitigate the transition from generalization to memorization and alleviate model collapse.

## Replace vs. Accumulate Scenarios

A critical distinction emerged in recent work: Under a 'replace' scenario where models are trained only on synthetic data from their preceding model, models successively degrade. However, in an 'accumulate' scenario where each training uses all real and synthetic data generated so far, collapse can be avoided.

Sophisticated iterative mixing strategies can mitigate model collapse. Using filtered synthetic data by a verifier yields clearer results and prevents mode collapse compared to retraining without verification.

## Data Curation and Diversity

Rather than accumulating all synthetic data, it is recommended to actively curate which synthetic data to include in your training set based on what the model needs. Metrics like maximum mean discrepancy or entropy can ensure the synthetic data adds new information rather than just amplifying existing patterns.
